Film these · three reels

Scripts you can read off the phone

Each one is a single take, about thirty seconds, written the way you actually talk: clear plan, honest numbers, no sugarcoating. They open on the surprise and then earn it, so nobody has to wait through a setup. The cover is your first frame.

Reel 01 · Same Door · ~30s

“Renting this apartment: twenty-five hundred a month. Owning the exact same apartment: about twenty-six fifty-eight. I can say that because both listings are mine. So here’s the honest math. Twenty percent down at today’s rate, property taxes, insurance, and the association dues. All of it. About twenty-six fifty-eight. And roughly two hundred twenty-four of that first payment stays yours, which rent never does. Before maintenance and transaction costs, that is about sixty-six dollars less in first-month cost. Treat it as an estimate; your numbers will differ. If that gap surprised you, ask me for 124.”

Option A · $2,500 to rent it. About $2,658 to own it. Same apartment, both listings mine. Full math in my Same Door carousel, sources included. The total is illustrative, not a quote. Write “124” for the breakdown.
Option B · $158 more cash. Roughly $224 becomes principal. The real first-month comparison, before maintenance and transaction costs. Ask for “124” for the breakdown.
Reel 02 · The $620 · ~30s

“Six hundred twenty dollars and thirty-one cents a month. Those are the association dues shown on this listing. They buy the pool, the gym, the water, the trash, the building’s insurance, so it’s not a trick. But leave it out of your math and the whole comparison falls apart, which is exactly what happens to most first-time condo buyers. They find the number after they’ve already fallen in love. So whatever you’re looking at, mine included, ask for the financials before you write the offer. Message me 124 and I’ll send you the list.”

Reel 03 · по-русски · ~25s (your pass first; I wrote it to read like a transaction, you’re the native speaker)

“Снимать эту квартиру — две тысячи пятьсот в месяц. Владеть той же самой — примерно две тысячи шестьсот пятьдесят восемь. Считаем честно: взнос двадцать процентов, сегодняшняя ставка, налоги, страховка, взносы ассоциации. И часть платежа остаётся вашей — аренда так не умеет. Это оценка, ваши цифры будут другими. Хотите полный расчёт по-русски — напишите мне «124».”

Post this week · two more carousels

Beyond the listing

Two pieces that keep working when there’s no inventory to post. Each one walks a single argument from the first slide to the last, so nobody drops out halfway. Sellers first, buyers second, each with its own keyword, so a save can become a conversation.

Seller copy · keyword NET
A · Your neighbor sold for asking. They probably still wrote a check. More than half of Valley sellers this spring handed money back at the closing table, around $25,000 on average, and none of that shows up in the price they tell you at the mailbox. So if you’re thinking about selling, ask what you’d keep before you ask what you’d list for. Write “NET” and I’ll put your number on one page. (SFV April 2026 closed sales, MLS compilation.)
B · The list price is a headline. The net sheet is the story. In April, over half of Valley sales carried a median $25,000 concession that no headline mentioned. Ask me for “NET”, no listing agreement attached.
Buyer copy · keyword CLOCK
A · The day your offer gets accepted, three deadlines start running and nobody hands you the dates. Seventeen days, seventeen days, twenty-one. Calendar days, so weekends count against you. None of it is scary once someone shows it to you, which takes about ten minutes. Save this for your next offer, and write “CLOCK” if you want yours mapped before you write.
B · The C.A.R. contract gives you three protections, and every one of them expires on a schedule. Slide two is the schedule. Write “CLOCK” and I’ll date every deadline for your exact timeline, in English or по-русски.
Film today · talking head, one take, no b-roll · keyword DOCS

“For sixteen years my job was reading the documents nobody else wanted to read. Litigation support. Research, analysis, the fine print. Then I got my real estate license, and the first thing I noticed was that everyone spends the whole time on the tour. But the tour isn’t what protects you. The paperwork is. The HOA financials, the disclosures, the board minutes, the deadlines. So that’s the part I never rush; I already spent sixteen years there. If you want someone who actually reads what you’re signing, in English or in Russian, write the word DOCS.”

Before anything posts

The don’t-say list

  • Never describe a neighborhood or building by who lives there. Speaking Russian is a service you offer, never a description of an area, in either language.
  • Keep “estimate, not a quote” wherever the $2,658 appears. Rate, credit, insurance, taxes, and association changes all move it.
  • Don’t say owning is simply cheaper than renting. Separate cash payment from first-month cost and name what the estimate excludes.
  • The $620.31 is the figure shown on the active unit-124 listing. Confirm it against current association documents before publishing.
  • No “guaranteed,” no “always appreciates,” no “can’t lose.”
  • If you boost any of it, never target by language or demographics. Housing ads follow special rules on every platform.
Two upgrades, when you’re ready
